title: Stormy seas in Carina
caption: The nebula NGC 3199, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
celestial: NGC 3199 · constellation Carina · about 12000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A crescent-shaped cocoon of gas and dust seems to plough through a star-studded sky, like a ship in stormy seas. The comparison suits its location. NGC 3199 lies in Carina, a southern constellation named after the keel of a ship, about 12,000 light-years from Earth.

Inside the nebula is HD 89358, an extremely hot and massive Wolf-Rayet star. It drives fierce stellar winds and outflows that crash into the surrounding material and sweep it up, which helps give NGC 3199 its twisted, lopsided look. Astronomers now know the bright crescent belongs to a far bigger, dimmer bubble of gas and dust.

John Herschel discovered the nebula in 1834 while compiling his catalogue of interesting night-sky objects. Since then it has been observed many times, including with ESO's 8.2-metre Very Large Telescope. This image comes from its smaller neighbour, the 2.6-metre VLT Survey Telescope.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (53.05 x 38.15 arcminutes) and distance (12000 light years), the frame spans roughly 185 × 133 light-years. Its light set out about 12,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope's OmegaCAM camera recorded this visible-light image through g, r and i filters and a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour mapping isn't published.

explore: The VST began operations in 2011. Its 256-megapixel camera, OmegaCAM, can photograph an area of sky twice the size of the full Moon at once. That lets it survey interesting objects which the Very Large Telescope can then study in even more detail.
alt: A crescent-shaped cloud of gas and dust moving across a field packed with stars.
